supplementary_news.content: Florida Is Confronting Yet Another Surging Viral Threat: Dengue Fever Another day, another potentially deadly virus circulating in Florida as helicopters pass overhead, spraying pesticides. Update: The very day this post went live, came news of what might be the Tampa area's first confirmed death from dengue fever in nearly a century. According to the Tampa Bay Times, an otherwise healthy 80-year-old woman named Gay Small contracted what is believed to be dengue locally. She had not traveled or left the city limits in more than a month, according to her daughter, and usually walked at least five miles per day in the city. The Florida Department of Health has not yet confirmed the dengue diagnosis and fatality, but this seems likely to be a grim precedent for the state. Another day, another potentially deadly or debilitating virus to worry about for America's Florida snowbirds, where dengue fever is seeing another one of the concerning surges that have characterized the state in recent years. The mosquito bite-driven infection is a persistent blight on tropical locales such as Latin America and the Caribbean, but is increasingly making itself at home in the United States as well ... particularly in the Sunshine State, which is again leading the United States in dengue infections throughout 2026, according to recently updated CDC data. The specter of the disease is increasingly difficult to ignore, particularly for the residents of Tampa who sound just a little bit concerned about the helicopters now passing over their heads spraying pesticides on the city, in an effort to interrupt the mosquito life cycle before the outbreak gets worse. When you've reached the "indiscriminate spraying of poison" stage, the time for pretending a problem doesn't exist has clearly passed. The virus-causing dengue fever is suspected to have been around for going on 2,000 years at this point, and as far as we know it is entirely spread by female mosquitos of the genus Aedes. Said mosquitos were actually largely eradicated in Central and South America in the 1950s, but when those eradication programs were allowed to lapse, the disease returned with a vengeance by the 1980s and has been hyperendemic throughout the region ever since. Epidemics of dengue, meanwhile, are particularly possible because there's a very wide range of outcomes in infection: Some people show no symptoms at all, while others became severely ill. Classic symptoms include sudden fever, severe headaches, eye pain, debilitating joint pain, and gastrointestinal bleeding, with some cases progressing to hemorrhagic fever that can be fatal. If treated, only about 1% of dengue cases are expected to be fatal, but the disease can still be a nightmare to endure. And any infected person, if bitten by a mosquito, can ultimately spread the virus to many others. Most dengue cases in the U.S. are brought home by Americans who have traveled abroad, a pattern that has been in place for decades. In the last 15 years, this has typically involved annual cases in the range of 400 to 800, with only a tiny amount of transmission actually occurring in the United States. Since 2023, however, global dengue cases have surged, at least partially driven by a complex net of effects tied to climate change–warmer temperatures, for instance, decrease the time that it takes for a mosquito to become infectious after biting an infected person. And as cases in vacation destinations in Central America, South America, and the Caribbean have climbed, that has also led to a surge of dengue cases making their way back to the U.S., which in turn increases the risk of more local U.S. transmission. Cases in the U.S. shot all the way up to 3,352 in 2023 and 3,767 in 2024, before declining somewhat to 1,482 in 2025, a total that is still much higher than the recent average. This year's cases are climbing once again, however, with the CDC putting the U.S. at 1,735 cases with a third of the year still left to go. Note, those numbers exclude U.S. territories like Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands and American Samoa, where dengue is endemic. No other state in 2026, meanwhile, has had even a fraction of the dengue fever cases of Florida, which the CDC puts above 200 at this point. Most concerningly, that involves at least 60 statewide cases that are believed to have involved local transmission, which means quite simply that Aedes mosquitos are successfully biting people in the state who are infected with dengue and then spreading the virus to new hosts. Hence, the helicopters now circling Tampa, spraying what local governments are referring to as "ultra-low volumes" of pesticides in an effort to break the mosquito spread and interrupt the chain of infection. One wonders, given the state's MAGA leanings and tendencies toward misinformation on topics like vaccines and reproductive medicine, how its residents feel about a mass-pesticide campaign. Residents are apparently being told to stay indoors during spraying, and to do their part by dumping out any containers of standing water on their property where mosquitos are able to breed. "The application method that we're supplementing here using the orange helicopter... has been proven really effective during dengue transmission with Aedes aegypti specifically," said Adriane Rogers of the Pasco County Mosquito Control District. "When using this method in conjunction with our other control tools, we will be able to stop this. This is going to take several weeks of interruption to that mosquito life cycle, to really get mosquito populations low enough that it can no longer sustain disease transmission." I know it's asking far too much to even suggest this, but such a pox descending on our Floridian doorstep really should generate a new degree of empathy for one of America's other near neighbors, Cuba, which has been utterly savaged by both dengue and the similar Chikungunya virus also carried by the same genus of mosquitos. Just 90 miles off Florida's coast, the aftereffects of hurricanes, rolling blackouts and canceled trash collection have led to overwhelming amounts of mosquito-borne disease, which have infected potentially millions of Cubans in the course of the last year while the Trump administration has turned a completely blind eye to the suffering it has helped exacerbate. Like dengue, chikungunya can cause sudden high fever and debilitating joint pain that can leave sufferers unable to stand or walk. And guess what? The CDC estimates that more than 100 U.S. travelers have also come down with chikungunya this year as well. How long before we bring that one back to the homestead for some local transmission as well? Before too much longer, the mosquito-borne menace that has crippled Cuba may well be our own problem to deal with. But hey, maybe Florida has it all under control? Considering where the state's funds designated for healthcare have actually ended up in recent years, I wouldn't count on it

Learn more Build your reading streak0/3 today·Counts at 25% Peru's largest public health insurer has placed its national network on alert for dengue weeks before El Niño rains arrive, moving to avoid a repeat of the record 2023 epidemic that killed hundreds of Peruvians. EsSalud, the state-run Seguro Social de Salud that covers millions of insured workers and their dependents, has reinforced dengue surveillance across the country, according to the Peruvian state news agency Andina. The insurer warned that rains, higher temperatures and accumulating water are creating favourable conditions for the Aedes aegypti mosquito, which transmits the virus. Why El Niño Multiplies the Risk El Niño is a natural warming of sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific that reshapes rainfall patterns across the Americas. In Peru, past events have brought torrential coastal rain and flooding, and the standing water left behind becomes a nursery for Aedes aegypti, a mosquito that completes its breeding cycle in as little as seven days. The global context gives the warning weight. Dengue has become the world's fastest-spreading mosquito-borne disease, and the World Health Organization estimates that about half of the world's population is now at risk. Cases reported to WHO rose from roughly 500,000 in 2000 to 5.2 million in 2019, and the organization has repeatedly linked warming temperatures and shifting rainfall to the insect's expanding territory. WHO also notes there is no specific treatment for dengue, making early detection and vector control the backbone of prevention, particularly in Latin American and Asian countries where severe dengue is a leading cause of hospitalization. A Country That Knows the Cost Peru is not bracing for an abstract threat. The country endured its worst dengue epidemic in recorded history in 2023, when data from the Pan American Health Organization show more than 270,000 cases and more than 400 deaths. The government of President Dina Boluarte declared a state of health emergency in June 2023 as hospitals in Piura, Lima and other regions came under severe strain, with the northern coast among the hardest hit. The precedent stretches further back. During the 2017 El Niño Costero, floods destroyed infrastructure across Peru's northern coast and dengue cases surged past 180,000, according to PAHO figures. The pattern is consistent: each major El Niño event has been followed by a spike in the disease. Reported dengue burden in Peru during recent crisis years, according to Pan American Health Organization data Year Reported cases Context 2017 More than 180,000 Surge after El Niño Costero flooding on the northern coast 2023 More than 270,000 Worst epidemic in Peru's recorded history, with more than 400 deaths What the Reinforced Plan Involves According to Andina, the reinforced surveillance is national in scope and aims to detect and treat cases early, before peak rains amplify transmission. The report framed the deployment as a preventive measure rather than a reaction to an outbreak already under way, citing the health risk that El Niño poses to the population. Specific staffing numbers, budget allocations and the list of priority regions were not detailed in the initial announcement, and those specifics remain under independent verification. EsSalud operates hospitals and outpatient clinics across all of Peru's regions, giving the insurer capacity to run early-warning triage alongside the Ministry of Health's vector-control teams. Effective prevention rests heavily on the community. WHO guidance emphasizes eliminating standing water in tires, tanks, gutters and other containers where the mosquito lays its eggs, alongside fumigation campaigns and prompt medical care for suspected severe cases. A Warning That Crosses Borders The risk extends well beyond Peru. Heavy El Niño rains in late 2023 and early 2024 killed at least 180 people in Kenya and displaced hundreds of thousands, and the same flooding pattern suits Aedes aegypti. Kenya's coastal counties, including Mombasa and Kwale, have recorded recurrent dengue outbreaks that the Kenya Medical Research Institute has confirmed in past seasons. Health systems in both hemispheres are confronting the same equation. WHO has warned that climate change is pushing dengue-carrying mosquitoes into areas with little population immunity and no established surveillance, which makes early investment in detection the difference between an outbreak contained in weeks and an epidemic that fills hospitals. EsSalud's bet is that vigilance bought now is cheaper than treatment bought later. Within months, El Niño will either arrive as forecast or spare the Pacific coast. Home Business Lifestyle Tutorials Technology Politics Education Sports Public Info Automotive Opinion Economy Health Discover more Public Health Biological Sciences Beaches & Islands Home Health Florida Mosquito Control Ramps Up Effort as Dengue Cases Surge Florida Mosquito Control Ramps Up Effort as Dengue Cases Surge Jessica Williams Published Sep 8, 2026 - 02:40 7 Reads Last Update Sep 8, 2026 - 02:40 Share WhatsApp Smallest Font Largest Font Florida mosquito-control agencies are escalating surveillance, inspections, and spraying operations as health officials prepare for a surge in locally acquired dengue fever cases across Tampa Bay and the entire state, according to local reports. As of September 1, local health data revealed that state-wide dengue cases originating within Florida rose to 41, with 33 recorded in the Tampa Bay region. Local transmission indicates patients contracted the mosquito-borne virus in their home areas rather than during foreign travel. The Florida Mosquito Control Association confirmed 30 cases in Hillsborough County, seven in Miami-Dade County, three in Pinellas County, and one in Palm Beach County. Health officials subsequently placed both Hillsborough and Pinellas counties under official mosquito-borne illness alerts. Highlighting the widespread regional threat of the virus, officials emphasized that geographic boundaries offer no protection against local transmission. "Dengue does not stop at county lines," Pinellas County Mosquito Control Director Alissa Berro said. Officials noted that while the primary mosquito vector travels within a narrow range, daily human commute across counties facilitates broader spread. When mosquitoes bite infected travelers, they can subsequently transmit the virus to residents in neighboring communities. "The mosquitoes that transmit the virus generally stay within a relatively small area, but people travel throughout the Tampa Bay area every day. When someone infected with dengue enters a new area, a local mosquito can bite that person and later spread the virus to others. As cases rise across the region, so does the potential for additional local transmission," Berro said. Control crews have stepped up aerial and ground treatments targeting areas with active viral transmission while conducting property inspections. The Florida Mosquito Control Association urges residents to clear standing water from containers, wear light-colored long clothing, and use insect repellent containing DEET or approved alternatives. The outbreak follows a record-setting 2024, during which the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported 3,798 dengue cases across U.S. states and Washington, D.C. Florida led the nation that year with 1,044 total cases and 85 locally acquired infections across 10 counties. Experimental Monoclonal Antibody Shows Therapeutic Promise Against Dengue: JAMA Subscribe to Notifications Written By : Dr Riya Dave Medically Reviewed By : Dr. Kamal Kant Kohli Published On 2026-09-07 15:00 GMT | Update On 2026-09-07 15:00 GMT An experimental monoclonal antibody for dengue virus was found to be safe and well tolerated in a phase 2 clinical trial, with findings also providing early evidence of a potential therapeutic benefit, according to a study published in JAMA Network Open. The study was conducted by Prasad S. and fellow researchers. To determine the safety profile, pharmacokinetics, and antiviral activity of Dengue-mAb, a randomized, single-blinded, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial was undertaken between September 19, 2021, and May 13, 2023, at 12 hospitals in India. Inclusion criteria for participation included adults in the age range of 18 to 60 years with dengue infection and fever beginning within 48 hours prior to enrollment. Exclusion criteria for participation in the study included presence of severe signs and symptoms of dengue, hemoglobin level below 10 g/dL, absolute neutrophils count below 500/mm3, total leukocytes count less than 1500/mm3, and platelets level below 50,000/mm3. Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1:1:1:1 ratio through an interactive web response system for administration of a single intravenous dose of placebo or Dengue-mAb with doses of 3 mg/kg, 5 mg/kg, 7 mg/kg, and 9 mg/kg. Main endpoints involved evaluation of viral log reduction at 24 hours and serious adverse events (SAEs). Secondary endpoints were complete RNAemia resolution, fever duration, and hematological parameters. Data analysis was conducted between January 11, 2024, and March 26, 2024. Key findings: The clinical evaluation of 250 randomized patients (median age 30 years [IQR, 24–37]; 72.3% male [180/250]; 50 participants per group) demonstrated significant antiviral, fever clearance, and safety results. Zero causally related serious adverse events were observed across all dose tiers, establishing high safety and tolerability. Adjusted mean (SE) viral log reduction at 24 hours was significantly greater with Dengue-mAb, ranging from 1.93 (0.23) at 3 mg/kg (P = 0.04) to 2.35 (0.27) at 9 mg/kg (P = 0.003), compared to placebo (1.29 [0.22]). Patients with detectable viremia at baseline (n = 32) achieved negative viral status by 8 hours when treated with 5 mg/kg to 9 mg/kg of Dengue-mAb, compared to 72 hours in the placebo cohort. Fever cleared in a median of 3.5 hours (95% CI, 1.0–24.0; HR, 2.6 [95% CI, 1.0–6.4]) at 5 mg/kg (n = 14) and 2.0 hours (95% CI, 0.5–6.0; HR, 2.8 [95% CI, 1.2–6.8]) at 7 mg/kg (n = 14), compared to 26.8 hours (95% CI, 1.0–50.5) with placebo (n = 12). At 24 hours, fever resolved in 92.9% (13/14; 95% CI, 66.1%–99.8%) at 3 mg/kg, 100.0% (14/14; 95% CI, 76.8%–100.0%) at both 5 mg/kg and 7 mg/kg, and 94.1% (16/17; 95% CI, 71.3%–99.9%) at 9 mg/kg, compared to 58.3% (7/12; 95% CI, 27.7%–84.8%) with placebo. In summary, the single dose of Dengue-mAb administered intravenously was safe and highly effective in adults with acute wild-type dengue virus infection. The key points from the study include the fact that the ideal doses of 5 mg/kg and 7 mg/kg can induce fast suppression of viral infection as well as the rapid disappearance of fever, which makes Dengue-mAb an innovative drug in antiviral therapy. Reference: Kulkarni PS, Potey AV, Gupta SK, et al. Safety and Preliminary Efficacy of Dengue Monoclonal Antibody in Adult Patients: A Randomized Clinical Trial. Hospitals across the nation are overwhelmed by a sharp rise in cases, particularly in September, fueling fears of further intensification in the coming weeks. With dengue cases reported across all 64 districts, government initiatives aim to curb the spread through preventative measures. supplementary_news.content: Dengue fever is spreading. Here are 5 tips to help avoid it. For the first time in almost a century, Tampa Bay is experiencing an outbreak of dengue fever. The tropical disease, which doctors thought had almost been eradicated in the United States, is now buzzing through our backyards. Hillsborough County is the epicenter of this summer's epidemic. By the end of August, 59 people had been hospitalized after contracting infections locally. Most cases are mild. But in some people, the virus can be deadly. On Friday, a Tampa woman became the first local person to die after contracting dengue,her daughter said. Mosquito control teams are working overtime, adding aerial, truck and spot spraying, inspecting people's property. But the best defense against the two most dangerous species of insects, experts say, is the public. Here are five ways to help slow the spread of the disease — and protect yourself: Keep things dry Dump out rain water from garbage cans, gutters, flower pots, pool covers and toys at least weekly. Even bromeliads can be breeding grounds for mosquitoes. The Aedes aegypti species, which carries dengue, can lay 100 larvae in a bottle cap. Clean bowls, dishes, ponds Empty and wipe out bird baths and pet water bowls at least twice a week. Larvae can linger long after a container is drained. If you have a turtle pond or horse trough, you can pick up mosquito-eating fish to add from the Pinellas and Hillsborough county mosquito control offices. Check your tires Discard outside trash and tires — which are the mosquitoes' favorite place to breed. Look out below Wear long pants, socks and shoes. The two scary species fly low, during the day, and love attacking ankles. Use bug spray Spray insect repellant on clothes and exposed skin. Mosquito experts recommend bug spray that contains DEET, picaridin or oil of lemon eucalyptus. Source: Hillsborough County Mosquito Management Services, Florida Department of Health

supplementary_news.content_title: Mathematical Modelling of the Impact of Misdiagnosis on Dengue-Malaria Co-Infection Dynamics
supplementary_news.content: Login Login 切换导航 Home Articles Journals Books News About Services Submit Home Journals Article Journal of Applied Mathematics and Physics > Vol.14 No.9, September 2026 Mathematical Modelling of the Impact of Misdiagnosis on Dengue-Malaria Co-Infection Dynamics () Eyaran Wilson Ewesit*, Mary Wainaina, Damian Maingi Department of Mathematics and Actuarial Science, Catholic University of Eastern Africa, Nairobi, Kenya. DOI: 10.4236/jamp.2026.149165 PDF HTML XML 0 Downloads 16 Views Citations Abstract Malaria and dengue fever are among the leading causes of Undifferentiated Febrile Illness (AUFI) which account for majority visits to the hospital in Africa. The diseases are spread through biting of mosquitoes making coifection a very common phenomena in tropical and subtropical regions due to high prevalence of mosquito populations. A common challenge of managing both diseases in Africa is misdiagnosis of dengue fever for malaria due to similarities in symptoms and limited resources for accurate diagnosis. This research focused on developing a mathematical epidemiological model to investigate the impact of misdiagnosis of dengue fever as malaria on the general spread dynamics of malaria and dengue fever. The analytical properties of the spread dynamics were studied. The model was determined to be mathematically well stated and biologically well posed by ensuring the positivity and boundedness of the solutions. The co-infection-free Equilibrium was determined to exist using the jacobian matrix method. The co-infection reproductive number was calculated using the next generation matrix approach. The existence of the endemic equilibrium was determined. The normalized forward approach was used to determine the sensitivity indices and identified the parameters that most likely to be targeted for control of the malaria-dengue fever coinfection spread dynamics. Numerical simulations were conducted to obtain the numerical values of the sensitivity analysis and the numerical solutions to the spread dynamics. Keywords Basic Reproductive Number, Coinfection Dynamics, Malaria-Dengue Fever, Equilibrium Points, Mathematical Modelling, Numerical Simulations Share and Cite: Ewesit, E. , Wainaina, M. and Maingi, D. (2026) Mathematical Modelling of the Impact of Misdiagnosis on Dengue-Malaria Co-Infection Dynamics. Journal of Applied Mathematics and Physics, 14, 3311-3330. doi: 10.4236/jamp.2026.149165. 1. Introduction The monoinfection of either malaria or dengue fever by itself is fatal, however, the coinfection of both diseases has been proven to be more fatal [1]. Since they are both spread by mosquitoes, their prevalence in Africa has become more prevalent [2]. The two diseases even share common signs such as fever, headache, myalgia, nausea, and diarrhoea. As a consequence, the coinfection of the diseases is either ignored or leads to misdiagnosis of coinfection as malaria since malaria is more pronounced when compared to dengue fever [3]. In resource limited countries such as Kenya, the probability of presumptive treatment of dengue fever as malaria is very high [4]. More so, coinfection is often is treated as a mono infection due to the clinical similarities in the manifestation of the disease. Misdiagnosis is more prone in coinfection spread dynamics than in regions that have a prevalence of one disease. Concurrent infection often occurs and obscures the symptoms of either of the initial conditions and the treatment regime of coifection is not the same as the treatment of the mono infection of either disease. As a result, the delayed implementation of the correct treatment regime leads to complications that can be fatal [5]. Increased movement of populations arising from efficient transport systems is posed to further aggravate the situation by introducing the disease to new environments where the diseases were not prevalent leading to further coinfection. Malaria and dengue are the leading causes of Acute Undifferentiated Febrile Illness (AUFI), which is the most frequent reason for seeking healthcare services in Africa [6]. The World Health Organization (WHO) reported 263 million malaria cases across the globe with Africa accounting for 94% of the cases. The same reports indicated 597,000 deaths across the globe with Africa accounting for 95% of the deaths [7]. Dengue fever has also been in the rise in sub-Saharan Africa with around 200,000 suspected cases and 90,000 confirmed cases that resulted in 900 deaths [8] [9]. Most of the cases in Africa go unreported leading to inaccurate statistics. One of the key challenges of the management of both diseases is misdiagnosis which is more prevalent in Africa due to the prevalence of both types of mosquitoes that spread the disease [5]. As a result, this clinical gap presents an opportunity for research in mathematical epidemiological modelling of malaria-dengue fever coinfection. Therefore, this study focused on developing a mathematical model that investigates the coinfection dynamics of the two diseases in one geographical area. 2. Model Description and Formulation In this model, the total human population at any given time t, denoted by ( N h ) is divided in ten human beings sub-classes. These are susceptible humans ( S h ) , individuals exposed to malaria ( E m ) , individuals infected by malaria ( I m ) , and individuals who recover from malaria ( R m ) . On the other side, we have individuals exposed to dengue ( E d ) , individuals misdiagnosed ( M d ) , individuals infected by dengue ( I d ) , and individuals who recover from dengue ( R d ) . At the center of the model are individuals infected with malaria and dengue co-infection ( I c ) and individuals who recover from malaria and dengue fever ( R c ) . Susceptible humans are those that are at risk of developing an infection. Infectious individuals are those that have symptoms of either of the disease or both disease. Exposed individuals are those that have been bitten by an infected mosquito but have not become infectious. Recovered are those that show temporal immunity. Co-infection are those individuals that are infected with both malaria and dengue fever. Total human population is represented by N h = S h + E d + M d + I d + E m + I m + I c + R d + R m + R c A schematic presentation of the malaria dengue fever spread dynamics was presented in Figure 1 below. supplementary_news.content: Dengue cases soar 66pc, deaths hit 62 in Malaysia, almost double 2025 toll KUALA LUMPUR, Sept 9 — Dengue fever cases nationwide have increased sharply by 66 per cent with 65,979 infections recorded as of Epidemiological Week 35 compared with 39,616 during the same period last year, says Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil. The unity government spokesman said the issue was among those discussed at the Cabinet meeting today, with the number of deaths due to dengue also showing a significant increase. He said 62 cases of deaths due to dengue were recorded up to the 35th epidemiological week of this year, compared to 32 cases in the same period last year. "The Cabinet was briefed on the status of the dengue problem which showed a marked increase compared with the previous year's. "The cumulative death toll for 2025 to the 35th week of the epidemic was 32 cases, while for the same period in 2026 there were 62 cases and this is an increase of 93.8 per cent," he said at a press briefing that was broadcasted live after the Cabinet meeting in Putrajaya today. Fahmi, who is also the communications minister, said the Cabinet also discussed measures to address the hike in cases, including the implementation of gotong-royong programmes soon. He said the Housing and Local Government Ministry (KPKT) will be in charge of organising the programme, especially in areas identified as red zones or where an outbreak is occurring. "The KPKT will start the gotong-royong programme in the next few months, and this will be followed up with a statement from the ministry," he said. Meanwhile, Fahmi said the Cabinet was also briefed on the success of the Wolbachia mosquito breeding programme in Putrajaya. However, he said the Cabinet was also informed about the effects of "fogging" activities on Wolbachia mosquitoes, which are used as a method of dengue control. "The Wolbachia mosquitoes, which are capable of inhibiting the reproduction and spread of the Aedes mosquito dengue virus, can die during the 'fogging' process. "With that, efforts to promote gotong-royong programmes need to be given attention, especially in locations identified as high risk," he said. The Wolbachia mosquitoes are regular Aedes aegypti mosquitoes that carry a natural, safe bacteria called Wolbachia, which blocks them from spreading dangerous viruses like dengue, Zika, and chikungunya

Florida is experiencing an increase in dengue fever cases originated in-state, with 33 cases in Tampa Bay alone and 41 statewide as of Sept. 1. According to Fox 13 Tampa Bay, the Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) reported 30 cases in Hillsborough County, seven in Miami-Dade County, three in Pinellas County and one in Palm Beach County. Cases are expected to increase. The Florida Department of Health has placed Hillsborough and Pinellas counties under mosquito-borne illness alerts. Cases as Mosquito Threat Grows Posted by Chinenye on Tue 08th Sep, 2026 - tori.ng Health officials in Florida are stepping up mosquito control as dengue cases continue to emerge in several areas. (Mosquito Bites. Photo by New York Post) Mosquito control teams in Florida are stepping up efforts to fight dengue fever as health officials expect more cases in the coming weeks. As of September 1, Florida had recorded 33 locally acquired dengue cases in Tampa Bay and 41 statewide. ReserveIsland Resorts Locally acquired means people caught the illness at home, not while traveling. Cases are expected to keep rising in the next few weeks. Most cases are in Hillsborough County with 30 confirmed infections, followed by seven in Miami-Dade, three in Pinellas and one in Palm Beach County. Hillsborough and Pinellas counties are under mosquito-borne illness alerts. Dengue is spread by mosquitoes and causes fever, severe body aches, nausea, rash and sometimes serious complications. The virus is common in tropical areas like Southeast Asia, Latin America and Africa. Discover more Download Interactive Maps Order Infection Tests Hire Pest Exterminators It rarely occurs in the mainland US, but Florida, California and Texas have seen local transmission. Last year was a record year with 3,798 cases reported across the country, up 359 percent from the average between 2010 and 2023. Mosquito crews are spraying areas with dengue activity and checking properties for breeding sites. Officials are asking residents to get rid of standing water around their homes since the dengue mosquito lays eggs in buckets, plant pots, tires and other containers that hold water. Health authorities recommend wearing long sleeves, light colours and closed shoes outside. Use insect repellent with DEET or picaridin. Check your yard regularly and dump any standing water. Most people infected with dengue have no symptoms or recover within a week or two. But some develop severe dengue, which can be life-threatening. OrderInfection Tests Warning signs include severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unusual bleeding, trouble breathing and extreme tiredness. Anyone with these signs should get medical help right away. supplementary_news.content: Schedule NFL News Draft Fantasy Odds Betting Newsletter STATE Florida dengue cases spike. How to protect yourself on Labor Day weekend C. A. Bridges USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Updated Sept. 4, 2026, 1:53 p.m. ET Locally acquired cases of dengue fever have recently surged in Florida, with 73 cases reported as of late August. Dengue is a mosquito-borne virus that causes fever, severe headaches, and muscle pain. Hillsborough County is the primary hotspot, accounting for 59 of the state's reported cases. Locally acquired cases of dengue fever, a mosquito-borne disease related to the viruses that cause West Nile and yellow fever, have surged in Florida in recent weeks. As of Aug. 29, 73 cases have been reported in the state, up from 41 the week before, according to the latest arbovirus surveillance report from the Florida Department of Health. And it's happening just as millions of Floridians are planning beach and boat trips, amusement park visits, and backyard cookouts for the long Labor Day weekend. “As families across Florida prepare to enjoy Labor Day weekend, I encourage everyone to take few simple precautions to protect themselves and their families from mosquito bites,” State Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo said in an email alert. “Use insect repellent, cover up when possible, and remove standing water around your home. Individual prevention helps protect you and your community” Buy mosquito repellent at Amazon The hotspot is Hillsborough County, where 59 of the 73 cases were reported. The health department said that 14 mosquito pools located there tested positive for DENV-2, four of them in the last week. DENV-2 is a distinct case of dengue that spreads to humans. Initial symptoms were first reported in Hillsborough in July and August, according to the agency's latest county-level summary. The rest of the cases were in Miami-Dade (7), Palm Beach (1), Pasco (1), and Pinellas (5) counties. Dengue infection happens when you get bitten by one of two species of mosquito, Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. Both are found in Florida. Florida has also reported 136 cases from people who traveled to dengue-endemic countries in the two weeks before symptoms arose. Mosquito-borne illness advisories, which advise the public to be careful, have been issued for Alachua, Duval, Leon, Orange, Palm Beach, Pasco, and Walton counties. Mosquito-borne illness alerts, which means there is heightened disease activity warranting extra precautions, have been issued for Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, and Pinellas counties. In 2025, 62 cases were reported in four counties: Brevard, Hillsborough, Miami-Dade, and Pasco. Here's what to know before you head outside this Labor Day weekend. What is dengue? What are the symptoms? Dengue infections are spread by mosquitoes. Mosquitoes become infected with dengue after biting a person with the virus. Those infected mosquitoes then spread the virus to other people. "Dengue fever can be a painful, debilitating disease but is rarely fatal," the Florida Department of Health said. Symptoms appear three to 14 days after the bite of an infected mosquito and include: Sudden onset of fever Severe headache Eye pain Muscle and joint pain (giving the disease the nickname “breakbone fever”) Bleeding Gastrointestinal symptoms like vomiting and diarrhea may also be present in some cases. Dengue fever symptoms usually last four to seven days. In rare cases, dengue hemorrhagic fever can develop from dengue infection and can be fatal if not recognized and treated with supportive care. There is no treatment for dengue fever, but quick identification and management of symptoms can prevent it from becoming more severe. Where has dengue been reported in Florida? Is it spreading According to the Florida Department of Health, as of Aug. 29, there have been 73 cases of locally acquired cases of dengue reported: 59 in Hillsborough County 7 in Miami-Dade County 1 in Palm Beach County 5 in Pinellas County How to protect against dengue There is no dengue vaccine. Since dengue is spread through infected mosquito bites, you should avoid getting bit. Stay indoors in places with air conditioning and with window and/or door screens. If you must be outside when mosquitoes are active, cover up and use insect repellent on exposed skin and clothing. Use mosquito netting to protect children younger than 2 months old. The FDOH recommends using EPA-registered repellents with active ingredients including DEET, Picaridin, IR3535, Oil of lemon eucalyptus, Para-menthane-diol, or 2-undecanone, a plant-derived ingredient. It's also important to prevent mosquitos from breeding in the first place: Drain water from garbage cans, old tires, pool covers, or any other containers where water collects. Empty and clean birdbaths and pet water bowls at least once or twice a week. Protect boats and vehicles from rain with tarps that don’t accumulate water. Maintain swimming pools in good condition and ensure they are appropriately chlorinated. Empty plastic swimming pools when not in use. Stay aware of local advisories, and if you're traveling, check for any country-specific travel recommendations, health notices, and warnings. "Almost half of the world's population, about 4 billion people, live in areas with a risk of dengue," the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said. Once returning from an area with a risk of dengue, even if you don't feel sick, the CDC recommends taking steps to avoid mosquito bites for three weeks to avoid the chance of spreading it to other people. While dengue cases have remained significantly lower this year in comparison to previous years health officials said they are getting reports of surge of fever cases in different districts, prompting them to strategise its combative measures.The health dept has directed administrators of all govt health facilities to line list admitted dengue patients, share their address and family contact numbers with relevant civic bodies so that the latter can take corrective measures like identification and elimination of the source. District health administrators have been asked to ensure compliance of such patient line listing by private hospitals in a dedicated portal for the private hospitals.All health facilities have also been asked to share the status of daily footfall in fever clinics or camps with the health quarter in a special format while ensuring testing for such patients. These teams consisting doctors, nurses and paramedic personnel have been tasked to visit facilities with high dengue case load and support the management of patients in those facilities.All govt blood centres have also been asked to ensure availability of platelet. Health officials said that at present there is no surge in platelet demand but it was prudent to keep the blood banks ready in case there is a surge in serious dengue positive patients who might need platelet transfusion.“While the dengue positive count so far is only about 50% of what the state witnessed last year (during the same period) we are witnessing a slight uptick at present. Even as the number is likely to remain under control we expect further spike during the next few weeks. This guideline is not to panic but for taking action,” said a health department official.This year the state has registered around 4,500 dengue cases across the state and the vector-borne disease has claimed seven lives officially. supplementary_news.content_title: Orange County increases mosquito control efforts in Pine Hills after dengue case
supplementary_news.content: PINE HILLS, Fla. — Orange County Mosquito Control crews are increasing spraying and surveillance in Pine Hills after a locally acquired case of dengue was confirmed in the community. The Florida Department of Health in Orange County confirmed the human case on Sept. 2. The department and Orange County Mosquito Control are coordinating surveillance and prevention efforts while expanding targeted treatments in the affected area. “We were notified on Wednesday of this week that we had a confirmed locally acquired case of dengue in the Pine Hills community,” said Steve Harrison, manager of Orange County Mosquito Control. “In response to that, our mosquito control crews have increased treatments and surveillance in that area in order to minimize the risk of any future spread of this virus.” Harrison said dengue is spread from person to person through the bite of an infected mosquito, not through social interaction. The Aedes aegypti mosquito is the primary species that spreads dengue. Harrison said it often breeds in containers and standing water around people’s homes. Unlike mosquitoes that are most active around dusk and dawn, the Aedes aegypti mosquito is primarily active during the day. It can also bite throughout the day. The mosquito has a short flight range and typically stays within a few blocks of where it emerged. The county is therefore concentrating its increased control efforts in Pine Hills, where the locally acquired case was reported. Orange County regularly conducts mosquito control efforts countywide. Crews use surveillance traps, calls from residents, field inspections and reported virus activity to determine where spraying is needed. After the Pine Hills case was reported, crews collected adult mosquitoes near the site and tested them using the county’s new in-house virus detection system. Harrison said none of the collected mosquitoes tested positive for dengue. Harrison said this is the third person to contract dengue locally in Orange County since 2024. The two cases reported in 2024 involved people from the same household. Residents can help reduce the risk by emptying water from potted plants, pet bowls, bird baths, and other containers around their properties. Harrison also recommends protecting against mosquito bites during both daytime and nighttime hours. Orange County said the chemicals it uses for mosquito control are approved by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and are safe for use around people and animals. Residents who notice increased mosquito activity can report it by calling 3-1-1

Communications Minister and MADANI Government spokesperson Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said the increase was among the matters presented to the Cabinet during a briefing on the latest status of dengue fever cases today. “Meanwhile, the cumulative number of deaths from dengue fever up to epidemiological week 35 in 2025 stood at 32, while in the same period in 2026, the figure was 62, representing an increase of 93.8 per cent,” he said at the weekly press conference after the Cabinet meeting here. Fahmi said as a preventive measure, the Ministry of Housing and Local Government (KPKT) would carry out large-scale gotong-royong programmes over the next few months as part of efforts to intensify measures to curb the spread of dengue. “At the same time, one of the matters discussed was the need to intensify efforts to organise large-scale gotong-royong activities, including in areas identified as red zones or where outbreaks have occurred,” he said. According to Fahmi, the Cabinet was also briefed on the success of the Wolbachia-infected Aedes mosquito breeding programme, including its implementation in Putrajaya. He added that Aedes mosquitoes carrying Wolbachia were able to inhibit the reproduction of the dengue virus, thereby reducing the virus’s ability to spread. However, he said fogging activities could have an impact on the programme. “When fogging is carried out, the Wolbachia mosquitoes are also killed. So, that is one of the matters that was highlighted,” he said. -- BERNAMA BERNAMA provides up-to-date authentic and comprehensive news and information which are disseminated via BERNAMA Wires; www.bernama.com; BERNAMA TV on Astro 502, unifi TV 631 and MYTV 121 channels and BERNAMA Radio on FM93.9 (Klang Valley), FM107.5 (Johor Bahru), FM107.9 (Kota Kinabalu) and FM100.9 (Kuching) frequencies. supplementary_news.content_title: Equip yourself with a 'double shield' to proactively respond to the peak season of dengue fever.
supplementary_news.content: Equip yourself with a 'double shield' to proactively respond to the peak season of dengue fever. As the peak of the 2026 rainy season approaches, the Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control and Prevention is continuously warning that the dengue fever situation is becoming more complex, with the number of cases steadily increasing. Báo Tin Tức • 07/09/2026 Doctors advise people to equip themselves with a "double shield" consisting of measures to eliminate mosquito larvae, prevent mosquito bites, and get vaccinated against diseases to protect their own health and that of their families. Many severe dengue fever cases have appeared. Khám phá thêm Đặt Vé Event Tra Bản Đồ tin Patients with severe dengue fever are being treated at the Adult Emergency, Intensive Care, and Toxicology Department of the Ho Chi Minh City Hospital for Tropical Diseases. (Photo: Dinh Hang/TTXVN) As the rainy season progresses, hospitals in Ho Chi Minh City are receiving an increasing number of dengue fever cases, many of which are severe and critical. Recently, the Children's Hospital of Ho Chi Minh City admitted two children in severe dengue shock. One of them, DTTV (10 years old, residing in An Giang province), was transferred with a diagnosis of severe dengue shock on the 5th day, with unmeasurable pulse and blood pressure. Doctors continuously administered intravenous fluids to combat shock, high-molecular-weight solutions, and vasopressors. However, the situation worsened, with the child experiencing blood clotting disorders, gastrointestinal bleeding, respiratory failure, and liver and kidney damage. In a critical condition, the patient was intubated and placed on a ventilator, and underwent hemodialysis and plasma exchange. Due to severe liver and kidney damage, the patient required 4 consecutive hemodialysis sessions and 3 plasma exchange sessions. After 3 weeks of intensive treatment, the child's health gradually improved. The second case involved HCK (7 years old, residing in Ho Chi Minh City) who was admitted to the hospital with abdominal pain, vomiting brown fluid, black stools, and cold extremities. Doctors diagnosed the child with severe dengue hemorrhagic shock on the 5th day, coagulation disorder, gastrointestinal bleeding, and severe liver damage. Despite receiving intravenous fluids, electrolytes, high-molecular-weight solutions, and shock treatment, the child's condition worsened, with significant ascites and pleural effusion, causing respiratory distress. Ultimately, doctors had to place the child on a ventilator, transfuse blood and blood products, and provide intensive respiratory support. After two weeks, the child regained consciousness, was weaned off the ventilator, and gradually recovered. You may also like Dengue fever affects not only children but also many adults. Recently, doctors at Gia Dinh People's Hospital had to work hard to save a pregnant woman suffering from severe dengue fever with complications of postpartum hemorrhage. Previously, Ms. NTML (23 years old, residing in Dong Nai City), 39 weeks pregnant, developed a high fever and was diagnosed with dengue fever. Because she was in the late stages of pregnancy, she was transferred to a specialized obstetrics hospital in Ho Chi Minh City for further monitoring and treatment. When she went into labor, she underwent a cesarean section; however, her health deteriorated rapidly, resulting in postpartum hemorrhage and severe coagulation disorders due to acute liver failure. She gradually fell into hemorrhagic shock, infection, uterine damage, and multiple organ failure before being transferred to Gia Dinh People's Hospital. Upon admission, she was in a deep coma, with low blood pressure, requiring intubation and mechanical ventilation. In the emergency situation, the leadership of Gia Dinh People's Hospital mobilized many specialties to participate in treatment. The patient received intensive resuscitation, blood transfusions and blood products, respiratory support, plasma exchange, treatment for liver failure, infection control, and correction of coagulation disorders. Due to severe uterine damage, along with infection and prolonged bleeding, the doctors were forced to perform a hysterectomy to control the bleeding source, treat the infection, and save the patient's life. According to Dr. Nguyen Tran Nam, Deputy Director of the City Children's Hospital, in recent years, due to climate change and urbanization, dengue fever has appeared year-round and increased sharply during the rainy season. In the past few months, the City Children's Hospital has received many cases for examination and treatment, including severe cases transferred from provinces in the Mekong Delta, Central Coast, and Central Highlands. The major difficulties in treating dengue fever currently are the late admission of patients when severe complications have already appeared, the confusion of symptoms with other illnesses, or the use of unproven folk remedies by family members causing bleeding and the risk of infection. Doctors warn that both adults and children are at risk of dengue fever if proactive preventive measures are not taken. In particular, overweight and obese children, pregnant women, the elderly, and those with underlying medical conditions are often at risk if they contract dengue fever, which not only threatens the patient's life but also increases the burden on the healthcare system. "Double shield" Remove water containers that harbor mosquito larvae to prevent dengue fever. Photo: Dan Phuong/News and Ethnic Minorities Newspaper According to Dr. Le Hong Nga, Deputy Director of the Ho Chi Minh City Center for Disease Control (HCDC), the city is entering the peak of the 2026 rainy season, notably with a continuous upward trend in recent weeks. The city has recorded over 1,000 new cases per week for four consecutive weeks. Specifically, in week 35 (August 24-30), the city recorded 1,256 dengue fever cases, a 4.4% increase compared to the average of the previous four weeks. The total number of dengue fever cases accumulated from the beginning of 2026 to date is 29,601 – higher than the same period in 2025. Of nearly 30,000 dengue fever cases, 16,430 cases required inpatient monitoring, care, and treatment at hospitals, accounting for 54% of the total cases, and more than 10,000 cases were treated on an outpatient basis at home. Localities with a high number of dengue fever cases per 100,000 people include Chanh Phu Hoa commune, Minh Thanh commune, and An Nhon Tay commune. You may also like Analyzing the reasons for the increase in dengue fever cases, Dr. Le Hong Nga stated that, according to epidemiological patterns, the number of dengue cases usually increases and peaks around October, then gradually decreases and drops to a low level around January and February of the following year, when the dry season becomes evident in Ho Chi Minh City. The increase during the rainy season stems from the biological characteristics of the Aedes mosquito – the vector of the disease. Unlike other mosquito species, Aedes mosquitoes only lay eggs in clean water environments, accumulating in household items such as buckets, basins, flower vases, offering bowls, or outdoor containers that collect rainwater. The rainy season creates favorable conditions for the increase of these stagnant water points. Epidemiologists believe that dengue fever is a consequence of climate change (rising temperatures, changing rainfall) and rapid urbanization, while waste management and water supply and drainage infrastructure have not kept pace. According to Master's degree holder and doctor Le Hong Nga, dengue fever has been and continues to be a global health challenge. Over the past 10 years, the number of cases worldwide has increased many times over, with an estimated 3.9 billion people living in at-risk areas. The World Health Organization (WHO) has developed a comprehensive strategy to control mosquito-borne diseases, requiring coordination between the government, the health sector, and the community. Therefore, a "double shield" is needed to prevent and control dengue fever in the community. People need to proactively equip themselves with two important layers of protection. The first layer is traditional environmental control measures such as mosquito eradication, eliminating mosquito larvae/pupae, and using methods to avoid mosquito bites. The second layer is using the dengue fever vaccine to create active and lasting immunity. Proactive vaccination helps reduce the incidence of the disease and minimizes the risk of severe illness, complications, death, or long-term sequelae if infected. supplementary_news.content: Play Now Log InSign Up Florida News Listen Live National News Weird News Local Traffic Local Weather Get News Alerts Florida News Hillsborough Leads Florida as Dengue Cases Double By Rob Garguilo Sep 4, 2026 Photo: martinatobolova / iStock / Getty Images Hillsborough County, FL - Florida health officials are tracking an increase in locally acquired dengue fever, with Hillsborough County reporting the highest total in the state. The county recorded 15 new locally acquired infections during August 16th through August 22nd, doubling its 2026 total from 15 to 30, according to the Florida Department of Health's latest surveillance report. Miami-Dade County added three cases during the same period, bringing its annual total to seven. Pinellas County had three locally acquired infections, while Palm Beach County had one. The state report listed 41 locally acquired dengue cases overall. Citrus County announced another case after the report's cutoff date. Health officials also detected dengue virus in four additional pools of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes collected in Hillsborough County. Ten mosquito pools tested positive in the county during August. A mosquito pool is a group of mosquitoes gathered from one area and tested together. Hillsborough County remains under a mosquito-borne illness alert. Local health and mosquito-control agencies are coordinating surveillance, inspections and treatments to reduce mosquito populations. Florida also reported 23 new travel-associated dengue cases during the week, raising the 2026 statewide total to 109. Those infections involved people who recently traveled to locations where dengue circulates. Dengue spreads primarily through the bite of an infected mosquito and does not normally pass directly between people. Symptoms can include fever, headache, severe muscle or joint pain, nausea, vomiting, pain behind the eyes and a rash. Residents are advised to use insect repellent, wear protective clothing, repair damaged screens and remove standing water from buckets, planters, tires, gutters and other outdoor containers where mosquitoes can breed. supplementary_news.content: Hillsborough County is Florida’s dengue epicenter as locally acquired cases rise Florida's surgeon general is calling Hillsborough County the epicenter of a growing dengue fever outbreak as health officials report a sharp increase in locally acquired cases across the Tampa Bay region. "Hillsborough County is really the epicenter of it," Florida Surgeon General Dr. Joseph Ladapo said during a visit to Tampa. The latest numbers show 65 locally acquired dengue cases across Hillsborough, Pinellas and Pasco counties, with 59 of those cases in Hillsborough County. Ladapo said more cases are expected. "So, we do expect to see more cases. We're at that point right now where we are seeing an increase in cases," Ladapo said. The locally acquired designation means the infections were transmitted by mosquitoes in the area rather than acquired while traveling elsewhere. Despite the rising case count, local officials say there are signs an aggressive mosquito-control response may be beginning to work. Hillsborough County mosquito control officials say no new human cases have been reported since the first aerial spraying mission earlier this week. They also estimate the adult female mosquito population has dropped by about 99% following three aerial missions. The county has significantly increased its mosquito surveillance, setting traps to track the population of Aedes aegypti mosquitoes, which can transmit dengue. "We want to immediately reduce the adult population," Hillsborough County mosquito control director Dr. Peter Jiang said. "Which is the ones already infected. Especially the ones already infected with the virus." The response has involved mosquito control, health officials and other county agencies sharing information to identify problem areas and quickly target them. "They can spot treat very quickly and right away thanks to that shared information," said Dr. Carla Fry of the Florida Department of Health in Hillsborough County. "That's just moving at light speed." Health officials say the response also includes an extensive community outreach effort. Fry said nearly 4,000 residents and almost 400 businesses have been visited in recent days, with crews providing information, repellent and larvicide while educating people about how to prevent mosquito breeding. But officials stress that spraying alone will not stop the outbreak. "If you have a tiny amount of water and containers underneath somewhere at your house, then the mosquitoes will keep coming," Jiang said. "More will emerge. That's why we require a full community effort." Officials are launching a public awareness campaign called "Spray, Cover and Drain." Residents are being urged to use mosquito repellent, cover exposed skin with long sleeves and pants when possible, and eliminate standing water around their homes. Fry said the advice is particularly important heading into a long holiday weekend, when more people are likely to spend time outdoors. "Wear repellent," Fry said. "That's really our biggest line of defense." She also urged people who will be outside for extended periods, such as while mowing the grass, to wear long sleeves and pants despite the heat. Dengue can cause fever, severe muscle and joint pain, headache, nausea and a rash. Health officials advise people experiencing symptoms to contact a health care provider and mention possible mosquito exposure

No, I am under 18 Yes, I am 18+ Home Info Sehat Indonesia Develops mRNA-Based Dengue Vaccine to Fight Four Virus Serotypes 07 September 2026, 14:25 | Editorial Team Dinno Baskoro Reporter Dinno Baskoro Editor The resource person who attended the Product Group Workshop and the Signing of the 2026 Innovation Cooperation Agreement at UI, Depok, Thursday, August 27. (doc. Etana) Share: JAKARTA - The development of health technology in Indonesia requires an ecosystem that is able to bring research results from the laboratory to become products that can be used by the community. One of the candidates being developed is a tetravalent dengue vaccine based on messenger RNA (mRNA) technology. The effort is part of a collaboration between the University of Indonesia (UI), the National Research and Innovation Agency (BRIN), the Education Fund Management Agency (LPDP), PT Etana Biotechnologies Indonesia (Etana), and Tsinghua University. In the Product Group Workshop and Signing of the 2026 Innovation Cooperation Agreement at UI, Depok, Thursday, August 27, Director of Corporate Relation & Strategic Affairs Etana, Andreas Donny Prakasa, said that biotechnology innovation is not enough to stop at the success of research. According to him, one of the biggest challenges in the development of biotechnology products is the valley of death, which is the phase when research results show potential, but are not ready to be developed into commercial products. The stages leading to a health product that can be used by the community require a long process. Research results need to go through scale-up development, validation, compliance with Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) standards, preclinical and clinical testing, as well as regulatory processes and market preparation. "The industry needs to be involved from the early stages of research so that market needs, production scale, regulations, and economics are considered. This is where the teaching factory plays a strategic role, as a place where research results are prepared to be upgraded from laboratory scale to industrial standards," said Donny. The research results of interest are mRNA-based tetravalent dengue vaccine candidates. The technology was developed considering the diversity of dengue viruses circulating in Indonesia. Representative of the UI dengue vaccine research team, Prof. Dra. Beti Ernawati Dewi, explained that the vaccine candidate was designed to cover four dengue serotypes, namely DENV-1 to DENV-4. The development was carried out by utilizing in silico mutation analysis as well as artificial intelligence approaches. These approaches are used to help design vaccine candidates that match the characteristics of local dengue strains. "The development of this mRNA-based dengue vaccine is part of an effort to bring innovations that meet Indonesia's needs, by utilizing the diversity of dengue strains circulating in the country," said Prof. Beti. Based on preliminary testing, the candidate showed neutralisation activity against all four dengue serotypes. Several vaccine constructs have also been reported to show better results than wild type and the commercial comparator Dengvaxia. However, the results of the initial research do not mean that the vaccine is ready for widespread use. The vaccine candidate still needs a series of research and testing stages to ensure its safety, effectiveness, quality, and feasibility before it can enter the stage of use in the community. Apart from technological capabilities and funding, the regulatory aspect is an important part of the health innovation journey from research to product. Representative of the Food and Drug Supervisory Agency (BPOM), Jeffeta Pradeko Putra, explained the BPOM GROW program (Green Research and Opportunities With BPOM). This initiative is designed to provide assistance to researchers in regulatory aspects, including the process leading to the production and registration of research products. "BPOM is committed to supporting the downstream of research from the beginning. Through collaboration between academics, businesses, and governments, we facilitate regulatory assistance to distribution permits so that Indonesian researchers' innovation products meet safety and quality standards, and are ready to provide real benefits to the community," said Jeffeta. Assistance from the initial stage is considered important because the development of biopharmaceutical products has complex safety and quality requirements. By understanding the regulatory needs from the start of the research, it is expected that technology development can run more directed. The development of vaccines and biopharmaceutical products requires time and large resources. Therefore, the success of downstream processing does not only depend on one party. The strengthening of teaching factory and laboratory facilities of universities needs to be linked to the Technology Readiness Level (TKT) or Technology Readiness Level (TRL). The mapping helps determine the position of an innovation as well as the stages that need to be taken before the technology can be further developed. Collaboration also needs to include funding, technology evaluation, testing, regulatory compliance, and commercialization readiness. In the context of health products, the Pentahelix approach is considered relevant because it brings together five elements, namely academics, industry, government, community, and media. Through the 2026 Product Group Workshop which took place on 27-28 August 2026, Etana together with UI and BPOM encouraged the strengthening of the research downstream ecosystem. A number of focuses include mapping TKT/TRL from the early stages, continuity of funding from research to commercialization, and increasing industry involvement in assessing the potential for developing research results. Forums that bring together researchers, industry, and regulators on a regular basis are also expected to shorten the distance between innovations in the laboratory and public health needs. For the development of dengue vaccines, this kind of ecosystem is important so that innovations that arise from research in the country do not stop as prototypes, but have a clear path to the testing stage, meeting standards, and ultimately can provide benefits to the community. supplementary_news.content: Latest Bhagwant Mann and Harpal Cheema join AAP political affairs committee MCD chairperson orders immediate action on unsafe buildings after Satya Niketan collapse Delhi government to establish separate engineering cadre for PWD after Centre’s approval BJD opposes MMDR Amendment Act, calls on President to intervene Pinarayi Vijayan defends daughter Veena over Cochin Minerals payments Telangana CM alleges ‘purification ritual’ near KCR farmhouse insults Dalits Thursday, 10 September About Contact ADVERTISEMENT Menu Home Opinion Politics Northeast India Arunachal Pradesh Assam Manipur Meghalaya Mizoram Nagaland Sikkim Tripura Nation & Beyond Visual Stories TNM Earth Business Startup TNM Buzz Sports Entertainment Cinema Music Home » Nation and Beyond » Delhi government holds workshop for MLAs and councillors on H1N1 and dengue prevention Nation and Beyond Delhi government holds workshop for MLAs and councillors on H1N1 and dengue prevention By TNM (With ANI Inputs) ✓ 7 September 2026, 7:52 pm 3 min read 7 Sep 2026 ANI Photo | Delhi government holds workshop for MLAs and councillors on H1N1 and dengue prevention The Delhi government convened a sensitisation workshop on September 7 to enhance awareness and prevention of H1N1 influenza and dengue among MLAs and councillors during the monsoon and post-monsoon seasons. The event, held at the Delhi Secretariat, involved elected representatives and senior health officials discussing the symptoms, prevention, early detection and management of the diseases. ADVERTISEMENT Stay connected Make The News Mill your preferred source See more TNM stories when you search for news on Google. Add TNM on Google Delhi Health Minister Pankaj Kumar Singh, who led the session, emphasised that prevention of seasonal diseases should not rely solely on hospitals and healthcare workers. He urged greater involvement from elected representatives, resident welfare associations, schools, markets and community organisations to communicate health messages directly to residents. “The aim is not to create panic, but to ensure that people have the right information and seek timely medical advice and care,” Singh stated. ADVERTISEMENT The minister cautioned against assuming that every fever is due to H1N1 or dengue, noting that common viral infections can also cause symptoms such as fever, cough and cold. He advised citizens to avoid self-diagnosis and to consult medical professionals as needed. Officials at the workshop highlighted basic measures to reduce the spread of seasonal influenza, including regular handwashing, covering the mouth and nose when coughing or sneezing, avoiding close contact with others when symptomatic, and using masks in crowded areas. Those who become ill were advised to rest, stay hydrated and seek professional medical advice rather than self-medicating with antibiotics or other medicines. ADVERTISEMENT Groups requiring special attention during the influenza season include children, the elderly and individuals with existing health conditions. Schools were encouraged to promote hygiene, cough etiquette and timely reporting of fever among students. The government also stressed preventing dengue by eliminating mosquito breeding sites. As the Aedes mosquito, which transmits dengue, can breed in small quantities of stagnant water, residents were urged to regularly inspect coolers, flowerpots, rooftop containers, water tanks, discarded items and tyres. Residents were instructed to keep water tanks and containers covered and to empty and scrub water-holding containers at least weekly. Removal of unused objects and waste that collect rainwater was also recommended. Singh asked MLAs and councillors to collaborate with resident welfare associations, schools, market groups, community organisations and sanitation teams to identify and address local mosquito breeding hotspots. Issues related to construction sites, drainage, waste accumulation and waterlogging should be reported promptly to authorities. The minister emphasised the importance of not ignoring persistent or high fever and seeking timely medical advice. Symptoms of dengue include high fever, headache, pain behind the eyes, muscle or joint pain, nausea, vomiting and skin rashes. While most patients recover, some may develop severe dengue requiring close medical monitoring. The government warned against self-medication and inappropriate use of antibiotics, advising that paracetamol may be used for fever or pain where appropriate but only under medical guidance. Officials also noted that the severity of dengue should not be judged solely by platelet counts. Singh assured residents that government health facilities in Delhi are equipped to manage seasonal diseases, with testing and treatment available for dengue and testing and isolation facilities for seasonal influenza. The broader objective of the workshop was to promote year-round community involvement in disease prevention rather than reactionary measures following outbreaks. Public representatives were encouraged to identify vulnerable areas within their constituencies, disseminate verified health information, monitor sanitation and mosquito breeding sites, and engage local organisations to mobilise residents. “The real success of this workshop will be when its message moves beyond this auditorium and reaches every ward, every neighbourhood and every household,” Singh remarked. He added that while the Health Department and field teams would continue their efforts, sustained community mobilisation will require active participation by elected representatives. The workshop formed part of the Delhi government’s preventive health initiatives under Chief Minister Rekha Gupta, aiming to strengthen coordination among elected representatives, health officials, field workers and local communities. supplementary_news.content: Health & Fitness Family Says Tampa Woman Died From Dengue Fever On 80th Birthday: Reports FL health officials are investigating the potential dengue fever death as cases are on the rise across Hillsborough County and the state. TAMPA, FL — The Florida Department of Health in Hillsborough County is investigating after the family of a Tampa woman who recently died reportedly said her death was caused by dengue fever, Claire Maher, public information officer for the department, told Patch. The department couldn’t confirm the death and said that under state law, the agency can’t provide details about specific cases, Maher said. Gay Small’s family told news outlets that she died early Sept. 4, on her 80th birthday, at Tampa General Hospital, where she was hospitalized with dengue fever. Find out what's happening in Tampafor free with the latest updates from Patch. Her case was locally acquired, her daughter, Anna Smalls, 55, told the Tampa Bay Times. “She hasn’t traveled. She doesn’t drive. She hadn’t left the city limits in more than a month,” Anna said. Find out what's happening in Tampafor free with the latest updates from Patch. Gay had been healthy and active before contracting dengue, her daughter told WFLA. “Cheated, just, you know, it’s so unfair because she was in good health and she worked hard to stay healthy and she walked and she ate right and you know, all the things that you’re supposed to do. And you know, this virus just kind of comes out of nowhere. She met the wrong mosquito, and that’s it,” Anna said. She and her family knew dengue well, as Gay’s late husband, Bob Small, spent his career working for pharmaceutical companies and nonprofits focused on developing a vaccine for the disease, the Times reported. Gay frequently traveled with him for work to Asia, South America and the South Pacific. If her cause of death is confirmed, it will be the first dengue fever death in the Tampa Bay area in nearly 100 years, reports said. Her death comes as dengue cases are on the rise across Florida, with Hillsborough County as the epicenter. More than 200 people in Florida have contracted the disease this year, according to the Florida Department of Health’s Florida Arbovirus Surveillance report for Aug. 23-29. The report is updated every Thursday. Seventy-three cases of locally acquired dengue have been recorded since Jan. 1, 59 of them in Hillsborough, the report said. There have also been seven cases in Miami-Dade County, five cases in Pinellas County, and one case each in Palm Beach and Pasco counties. The first locally acquired dengue case this year, reported in Hillsborough, was recorded in the July 19-25 report. Health department data also show that there have been 136 travel-associated dengue cases recorded in the state since the start of the year. The report doesn’t break down which county recorded these travel-associated cases. Rather, the data lists the country of exposure. According to the report, people who traveled to Cuba accounted for 101 of the travel-associated dengue cases. “Residents throughout the state should take precautions from mosquito-borne illnesses by appropriately applying insect repellent, avoiding areas with high mosquito populations, and wearing long pants and shirts when possible — especially during sunrise and sunset when mosquitoes are most active,” Maher said. Those experiencing dengue symptoms should contact their health care provider or local county health department, she added. See Also: Get more local news delivered straight to your inbox.
