supplementary_news.content_title: A Tampa woman was diagnosed with dengue fever. Within a week, she was dead.
supplementary_news.content: Gay Small was supposed to spend Labor Day weekend in North Carolina, taking long walks with her sister, picking apples with her grandkids. But she died at Tampa General Hospital early Friday, her 80th birthday. From a mosquito bite, her family said. Health officials have not confirmed the cause of death to the public, but that's what her kids say they were told. If so, Small would be Tampa Bay's first fatality in almost a century from dengue fever. She most likely caught it within a couple of miles of her condo on Bayshore Boulevard. "She hasn't traveled. She doesn't drive. She hadn't left the city limits in more than a month," said her daughter, Anna Small, 55. Gaywas healthy, her daughter said. The only pills she took were vitamins. She walked at least five miles a day, often along Tampa's Riverwalk. Since July, more than 200 Floridians have been hospitalized for dengue fever, far more than in any other state. The tropical disease normally is contracted when people travel overseas. But this summer, record numbers of people have been infected in Tampa Bay. The week before Smalldied, the number of locally acquired dengue infections in Hillsborough County doubled to 59. That's more than 10 times the cases of other Florida counties. The morning she died the Tampa Bay Times posted a story about the outbreak . A few hours later, the state's surgeon general held a news conference to warn the public. "Americans don't expect it to be here. But it's here," Anna Small said. "And for some people, it's really serious." In seven days, Gay Small went from feeling tired to her organs shutting down. Symptoms, then a diagnosis Come over for dinner, Gaytold her daughter on Friday, Aug. 28. I'll cook. She walked a couple of blocks from her condo to Publix. Bought salmon and salad fixings. Fruit for dessert. Her mom looked weary, Annathought. Drained, said Anna's husband, Philip Lenzen. They weren't worried. Maybe she was dehydrated from the heat. The next morning, Anna texted her mom: "How are you feeling?" The answer came back with misspellings, random letters. That wasn't like her mom, who had been a technical writer and prided herself on perfect copy. Anna finally deciphered the message: "I have a tremor." When Anna saw her mom that evening, Gay's hands were shaking. She was slurring, unsteady. Anna drove her to urgent care. The doctor there sent them to the hospital. At Tampa General, Anna had to help her mom out of the car. When Anna unlaced her mom's sneakers in the emergency room, she saw broken blood vessels snaking around swollen ankles. Nurses thought Gay might be having a stroke, so they ordered a CT scan. It came back normal. They ran tests on her lungs, liver, kidneys, spleen and heart, drew blood to screen for infections. Her mom hadn't been in a hospital in 50 years. Sunday morning, after Gay finally got a room, Anna went home to get some sleep. Her mom texted her and her husband a few hours later: "You are nothing goingnn To b elli gel." Anna's translation: You are not going to believe this. The next message, Gay typed, then corrected: "I have Denga Fever. Dengue!!!" "No way," Anna wrote back. "Well that's kinda good news. Who would have thought?" Anna Small, daughter of Gay Small, shows a picture of her mother at the beach. Gay loved walking at Fort DeSoto, picking up shells, photographing birds and clouds. A disease they knew Gay and her family know more about dengue than most Floridians. Her late husband, Bob Small, spent years working for pharmaceutical companies and nonprofits, trying to develop a vaccine for the disease, which infects about 400 million people around the world every year. She traveled with him for his work in Asia, South America, the South Pacific. Gay and her family knew you can't pass dengue between people, only through mosquitoes. Most who get the disease don't know they have it. Only one in four experience symptoms. They knew it can cause high fever, nausea, a rash — things that can be mistaken for the flu. In rare cases, they knew, the disease can cause debilitating aches, which earned it the nickname "breakbone fever." But they had no idea it was spreading in their backyards. "I considered the possibility of my elderly mom getting an acute illness or disease at some point," said Gay's son, Jeremy Small, 53. "But dengue fever? Without leaving her neighborhood?" Once Gay's family got a diagnosis, they were relieved. "We knew the odds of dying from dengue were really low," said Anna. With rest and fluids, they thought, their mom would be fine. Explaining the spread This summer, Tampa Bay's long drought followed by almost daily rain have helped spread the disease locally, said Kartik Cherabuddi, Tampa General's chief epidemiology officer. His staff has tested at least 10 times more people for dengue than they did last summer. After a bite, symptoms don't show for a week or two. When they do, doctors run a patient's blood through a tropical fever panel that can detect five different diseases, including malaria and dengue. Within six hours, they can make a diagnosis. So far, Tampa General has recorded 20 cases. Hospital officials said they can't comment on specific cases or verify the first dengue death. They report positive tests to the Florida health department, which updates a report on Thursdays. On Tuesday, Hillsborough's spokesperson for the state Department of Health, Claire Maher, said she couldn't confirm a fatality. About one-fourth of people with dengue get the severe form, which can cause internal bleeding. Doctors have to monitor patients' organs, watch for fluid pooling around the heart. "When the fever breaks and they start feeling better, that's the critical part," Cherabuddi said. Risk factors can worsen. "They have to keep being monitored." Most people, even with severe dengue, fully recover, he said. Around the globe, dengue kills an estimated 20,000 patients annually. Older people and those with preexisting conditions are more vulnerable. So are people who have had dengue before. With most viruses, the doctor said, people's immune systems build antibodies, so a second infection is milder. Dengue works the opposite way. There are four strains, so if you get a different type the second time, the antibodies try to attack it — which can cause more damage. Maybe Gay had gotten infected during her foreign travels and never knew it, Anna thought. Maybe that's why her case took such a tragic turn. Gay Small loved taking her two kids and six grandkids on exotic vacations to St. Thomas, Bonaire, France. Here, her daughter Anna shows off an album of a family trip to Curacao. A sudden downturn On Monday, the day after the diagnosis, Gay texted, "I'm not in great shape." Anna rushed to the hospital to find her mom's hands and feet scarlet and puffy. Plasma was building in her joints, a nurse explained. Gay's lactic acid was soaring. Anna called her brother in Atlanta: You better come. Jeremy found his mom having what he called a "sweat lodge moment — she's not making sense." On Wednesday, Gay's platelets crashed. Doctors gave her three blood transfusions. The next day, her heart rate soared while her blood pressure tanked. Doctors sent her to intensive care, where her kidneys failed, then her liver. Anna watched her mother grow jaundiced, so swollen she barely recognized her. While a helicopter hovered outside the hospital that afternoon, spraying insecticide to kill mosquitoes, Gay started gasping. "Please," she kept whispering, "can't we just go home?" Anna begged the doctor to be honest about her mother's prognosis. "We didn't want to keep her alive just to torture her." Unless you want to intubate her, the doctor told her, there's not much more we can do. Gay had signed a "Do Not Resuscitate" order years before. Doctors sedated her late Thursday, just before midnight, then turned off the machines. "It's almost her birthday," Anna told the nurses. "In eight minutes, she'll be 80." By daylight, she was gone. The aftermath On Sunday, Anna authorized an autopsy, which could show whether her mom had contracted dengue before. Her husband wrote the obituary. Gay and Bob Small had been married for 55 years. Besides writing, she'd knitted, done pottery, written poetry. She gave her daughter Gloria Steinem books; her son, Hunter S. Thompson's. She named her African grey parrot Will Shortz, after the New York Times crossword puzzle writer. "She was always active, kayaking, hiking and biking," Anna said. Fort DeSoto was her happy place. She was constantly photographing butterflies, birds and clouds. Generous and outspoken, Gay fed homeless people and fumed at teens racing e-bikes. She dabbled in massage therapy. Owned every Joan Baez album. Every summer, she took some of her six grandkids on grand vacations: Bonaire, St. Thomas, Curacao. Jeremy described her as "open, interesting, interested and extremely accepting." Three years ago, after Gay's husband collapsed during a bike ride and died, she moved from their Hyde Park home to the Bayshore condo, giving up her yard but not her gardening. She packed the patio of her 12th-floor unit with flowers. While she was in the hospital, drifting in and out of consciousness, she kept asking her kids, "Please, go water my plants." Over the weekend, the grandchildren who were going to meet in North Carolina to celebrate Gay's birthday gathered instead in their parents' South Tampa home. Gay's granddaughter baked the cake she had been planning: A lemon tart, Gay's favorite. They shared photos, reminisced about family trips, slathered on bug spray before walking to Armature Works for dinner. As they told stories, they shook their heads. Why did this happen to such a healthy, vibrant woman? How could she be gone? What good could come from her sudden death? Gay wanted, more than anything, to be useful, her daughter said, to make a difference. That's why her kids decided to share her story. "If she can let people know the severity of this," Anna said, "maybe it will give her death meaning."

Dengue Fever Surge in Tampa Bay: Helicopter Spraying Underway in Hillsborough and Pasco Counties By CAUDMedia - September 7, 2026 403 Facebook Twitter Pinterest WhatsApp Public health officials across the Tampa Bay area have escalated vector-control operations following a rapid rise in locally acquired dengue fever cases. Local health departments and mosquito control districts in Hillsborough and Pasco counties have authorized aggressive nighttime aerial spraying missions using low-altitude helicopters to target breeding vectors. With 65 locally transmitted infections confirmed across the Bay Area and at least 59 of those cases concentrated in Hillsborough County alone the region has become the epicenter of Florida’s current dengue response. What Is Dengue Fever? Understanding the Medical Condition Dengue fever is a mosquito-borne viral infection caused by any of four closely related dengue viruses (DENV-1 through DENV-4). It is primarily transmitted to humans through the bite of an infected female Aedes mosquito, predominantly Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus. Unlike airborne or respiratory viruses, dengue cannot spread directly from person to person through casual contact. Instead, a mosquito bites an infected individual during their viremic stage, acquires the virus, and subsequently transmits it to another person during future blood meals. 2315898467 Typical Symptoms Symptoms generally develop 4 to 10 days after an infective bite and often mimic severe flu-like illness: High Fever: Sudden onset of body temperatures exceeding 104°F (40°C). Retro-Orbital Pain: Severe, throbbing pain located directly behind the eyes. Musculoskeletal Pain: Intense joint, muscle, and bone pain (earning dengue its historical moniker, “breakbone fever”). Dermatological Symptoms: A distinctive maculopapular rash appearing 2 to 5 days after initial fever onset. Gastrointestinal Distress: Nausea, vomiting, and loss of appetite. 2481904799 What Doctors and Medical Experts Are Concerned About While most dengue infections resolve within 1 to 2 weeks with supportive care, medical professionals monitor these outbreaks closely due to two primary clinical risks: 1. Severe Dengue (Dengue Hemorrhagic Fever / Dengue Shock Syndrome) Approximately 1 in 20 patients infected with dengue progress to severe dengue after their initial fever subsides (the “critical phase”). Severe dengue causes plasma leakage, fluid accumulation, respiratory distress, severe bleeding, and organ impairment. Why Secondary Infection Matters: A primary infection provides lifelong immunity to that specific DENV serotype, but only short-term cross-protection against others. If a patient is infected with a different serotype later in life, antibody-dependent enhancement (ADE) drastically increases their risk of developing life-threatening severe dengue. 2. Warning Signs That Require Emergency Care Physicians advise residents to seek immediate medical intervention at an emergency department if any of the following warning signs appear: Severe abdominal pain or tenderness Persistent vomiting (at least 3 times in 24 hours) Bleeding from the gums or nose, or blood in vomit/stool Extreme fatigue, restlessness, or confusion Rapid breathing or difficulty breathing Current Dengue Situation in Florida While Florida frequently records imported, travel-related cases from travelers visiting endemic regions (such as the Caribbean or Latin America), locally acquired transmission indicates that infected mosquitoes are actively breeding and feeding within local communities. Aerial spraying missions in Hillsborough and Pasco counties utilize EPA-approved, ultra-low volume (ULV) adulticide applications during late evening and night hours. These operations aim to kill adult female Aedes aegypti mosquitoes before they can bite additional hosts. How to Protect Yourself and Your Family: The “3-Step Defense” The Florida Department of Health recommends a simple Spray, Cover, and Drain protocol to break the transmission cycle: 1. DRAIN Standing Water Around Properties Aedes mosquitoes breed in extremely small volumes of stagnant waterâ€”even as little as a bottle cap filled with rainwater. Empty water from flower pots, pet bowls, tarps, birdbaths, buckets, and discarded tires at least twice weekly. Clean clogged gutters and ensure swimming pools are properly chlorinated. 2. COVER Skin and Openings Clothing: Wear light-colored, loose-fitting, long-sleeved shirts and long pants when outdoors. Home Barriers: Keep windows and doors closed. Inspect window screens to ensure there are no tears or gaps. 3. SPRAY EPA-Registered Mosquito Repellent Apply insect repellent registered with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) containing one of the following active ingredients: DEET (concentration of 20% to 30% for extended protection) Picaridin IR3535 Oil of Lemon Eucalyptus (OLE) or PMD Stay safe and healthy always checking Newstalkflorida.com for updates on the latest news! Ad More Sports TBS Graduates Bangladesh Supplement Infograph Explainer Archive Gallery Long Read Interviews Offbeat Magazine Climate Change Health Cartoons বাংলা THURSDAY, SEPTEMBER 10, 2026 Chattogram doctors warn of dengue 'critical phase' as cases rise Health Sohanur Rahaman 04 September, 2026, 10:10 am Last modified: 04 September, 2026, 12:08 pm Related News Dengue cases likely to peak in late September, early October: Muhit Highest Dengue death, cases recorded in a single day this year PM to launch 3-month dengue prevention campaign on Saturday Dengue: 4 die, 1,314 hospitalised in 24 hours Dengue: Record 1,558 hospitalised in 24 hours, death toll reaches 117 Chattogram doctors warn of dengue 'critical phase' as cases rise Chattogram Medical College Hospital treating 78 patients; Chattogram dengue tally reaches 2,241 Sohanur Rahaman 04 September, 2026, 10:10 am Last modified: 04 September, 2026, 12:08 pm File Photo: Rajib Dhar A drop in fever does not always mean a dengue patient is out of danger, as the next 24 to 48 hours can be the most critical period for some patients, doctors in Chattogram have warned. The warning comes as Chattogram recorded 2,241 dengue cases and six deaths this year through yesterday, according to the latest data from the Civil Surgeon's Office. At Chattogram Medical College Hospital (CMCH), 78 dengue patients were admitted as of yesterday. Doctors said around 10 to 15 were in critical condition, while many were arriving with shock and bleeding. Keep updated, follow The Business Standard's Google news channel Professor Dr Anirudha Ghosh Joy, a medicine specialist at Chattogram Medical College, told TBS that it was difficult to predict which patients would suddenly deteriorate. "We cannot say in advance when a dengue patient will move into a critical condition. Keeping the patient under observation is therefore the most important thing," he said. Danger can begin when fever falls Dengue generally progresses through three phases—febrile, critical, and recovery. For some patients, the critical phase begins as the fever subsides and usually lasts 24 to 48 hours. During this period, fluid can leak from blood vessels, causing blood pressure to fall. In severe cases, patients may develop shock, bleeding, breathing difficulties, or complications involving organs such as the liver, kidneys, and heart. Anirudha said patients should not assume they have recovered simply because fever, body ache, or vomiting has eased. "Many think the patient has recovered once these symptoms disappear. But the period after the fever can be critical. Patients should remain under monitoring for at least three days," he said. Doctors advised seeking medical attention if patients develop severe abdominal pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, rapid breathing, unusual weakness or restlessness, reduced urine output, or falling blood pressure. Anirudha said platelet levels could also begin to fall towards the end of the fever period and should be monitored alongside the patient's overall condition and other warning signs. The Directorate General of Health Services' National Guideline for Clinical Management of Dengue, 5th Edition, 2025, says a platelet count below 100,000/mm3 can be an early indicator that a patient is entering the critical phase, when plasma leakage may occur. A rapid fall in platelets should also be assessed alongside rising hematocrit, reduced urine output, and other clinical signs. Some dengue patients in Chattogram are also presenting without severe fever or other commonly recognised symptoms, doctors said. Some report only mild fever, body ache, or weakness, while others mainly experience vomiting, abdominal pain, or loss of appetite. Doctors said some patients initially mistake these symptoms for ordinary fever, gastric problems or general weakness and delay testing until complications develop. Shock, bleeding cases rising at CMCH Doctors at CMCH said the growing number of patients arriving with severe complications had become a major concern. Dr Noor Mohammed, focal physician of the dengue ward at the hospital's medicine department, said many patients were arriving with shock syndrome and bleeding. "Most are coming with shock. This year, we are seeing patients whose blood pressure cannot even be recorded. Many are also coming with bleeding, while some have both shock and bleeding," he said. The hospital's specialised dengue ward has 40 designated beds, while 78 dengue patients were admitted to CMCH as of yesterday, according to the latest Civil Surgeon Office data. "The problem is not doctors at the moment. We are able to provide services. But as the number of patients rises, the facilities also have to increase. That is the main problem," Noor Mohammed said. He said additional beds, nursing support and other treatment facilities would be needed if patient numbers continued to rise. August alone saw 1,202 cases Dengue infections accelerated sharply in Chattogram from July. The district recorded 298 cases during the first six months of the year. Cases then rose to 536 in July and 1,202 in August. A total of 1,738 cases were recorded in July and August, nearly six times the number reported during the first six months of the year. Another 205 cases were recorded in the first three days of September, including 55 in the 24 hours to yesterday. Six people have died from dengue this year – one in February, two in July, two in August and one in September. Sitakunda records highest upazila cases Dengue has spread across upazilas as well as the city. Sitakunda recorded the highest number of cases among the upazilas, with 279 patients through yesterday. Sandwip had the lowest, with 12 cases. Shajedur Rahman said additional attention was being given to areas reporting higher numbers of patients, including Sitakunda. Upazila health complexes were being kept prepared for diagnosis and treatment, while health education activities were also being strengthened, he said. September remains a concern Health officials fear infections could continue to rise in September if rainfall, temperature and humidity remain favourable for Aedes breeding. Shajedur Rahman said eliminating Aedes breeding grounds remained the most important measure for preventing dengue. People should not allow water to accumulate in yards, rooftops, containers, old tyres or discarded materials, he said. October, warns State Minister Staff Reporter 6 Sep 26, 13:03 Save State Minister for Health Dr A M A Muhit has warned that the dengue situation could take a severe turn this season. He said there is a risk of a surge in dengue cases from the last week of September through October, urging everyone to remain vigilant before October to keep the situation under control. The state minister was briefing journalists in the parliament tunnel on Sunday afternoon, September 6. He said data analysis indicates that the dengue outbreak could intensify from the last week of September to October. Therefore, precautionary measures must be stepped up from now. If timely action is not taken, the situation could become alarming. The state minister said 13 deaths from dengue have been recorded this year so far, which is still lower than the previous year. However, he said field-level anti-dengue activities would be intensified from tomorrow, with public participation, to keep the situation under control. He said awareness campaigns will also be conducted on social media alongside field-level activities. Calling on the media to play a vital role in dengue prevention, he emphasised keeping all areas clean, including educational institutions and hospitals. The state minister specifically urged effective initiatives to keep the capital Dhaka free of mosquito breeding grounds. He said dengue prevention is not the sole responsibility of the government; preventive activities must be carried out at the field level with public involvement. (WWSB) - New CDC data show dengue cases have increased in several parts of Florida, including counties near the Suncoast. The CDC’s latest county list does not include Sarasota or Manatee counties. The agency does not show counties with fewer than three cases, so the report does not provide a current exact number for either county. Hillsborough County has 66 cases. supplementary_news.content: BACOLOD CITY — The City Health Office has reported three dengue deaths and three leptospirosis fatalities as of Aug. 22. Based on CHO records, the two most recent dengue fatalities were girls ages 4 and 5 from Barangays Granada and Mansilingan. Both victims died while confined at the Corazon Locsin Montelibano Memorial Regional Hospital. The older victim died Aug. 19 due to acute respiratory failure from severe dengue, while the younger victim died Aug. 21 due to multiple organ dysfunction syndrome from severe dengue. The two fatalities were added to the city’s dengue death toll, which earlier included a victim from Barangay Villamonte. A total of 448 dengue cases were recorded since January, with Barangay Mansilingan posting the highest number at 54. It was followed by Barangay Handumanan with 45 cases, Estefania with 40, Singcang-Airport with 30, Banago with 29, Alijis with 28, Villamonte and Granada with 24 each, and Tangub with 22. Despite the figures, the CHO noted a 40% decrease in dengue cases compared with 754 cases and five deaths recorded during the same period last year. Eight cases involved infants younger than 1 year old, while 179 involved children ages 1 to 10 and 133 involved those ages 11 to 19, for a total of 320 cases among people younger than 20. The CHO reminded residents to keep their surroundings clean and eliminate mosquito breeding sites, particularly during the rainy season. The Department of Health has also urged the public to search for and destroy mosquito breeding sites, use personal protection, seek early consultation for symptoms, and support fogging or spraying only in hotspot areas. (Glazyl M. Jopson via tdg photo by tdg)
